sections.explanation:
Capillaries are numerous microscopic blood vessels forming extensive branching beds, creating a large total area for exchange with tissues. Their narrow lumens place erythrocytes near the endothelium and slow passage through the network; most walls are a single endothelial-cell layer with a thin underlying basal lamina.

Dissolved oxygen and nutrients cross capillary walls into tissue fluid, while wastes can move toward blood along gradients. Some capillaries have fenestrations that increase permeability, for example at sites needing rapid fluid exchange. Fenestrations are not universally present, and capillaries do not all permit proteins to pass freely.

In intestinal villi, exchange is enhanced by extensive microvasculature. Thin endothelial walls and branching capillary beds support exchange.

sections.guidingQuestion: Recognize arteries and veins in cross section?
sections.explanation:
An artery usually has a relatively thick tunica media rich in smooth muscle and elastic material surrounding a more rounded lumen. A vein commonly has a thinner wall relative to its lumen and may look flattened in a histological section; many veins contain valves.

Both vessel classes have endothelial linings and outer connective tissue. Identify them by wall-to-lumen ratio and wall layers rather than by blood oxygen concentration, because pulmonary arteries carry relatively deoxygenated blood and pulmonary veins oxygenated blood. Section shape can be affected by tissue preparation.

Compare the thickness of a vessel's muscular wall to the lumen diameter. An artery carries blood away from the heart, with a thick resilient wall adapted to its pressure.

sections.explanation:
Each ventricular contraction sends a pressure pulse into the arteries. Their walls contain collagen for strength, elastic fibres to stretch and recoil, and smooth muscle that changes vessel diameter. A thick tunica media helps them withstand and maintain high pressure.

During systole arterial expansion temporarily stores energy; during diastole elastic recoil maintains forward flow while ventricular ejection pauses. Arteries carry blood away from the heart, not necessarily toward an oxygenated tissue. Excessive rigidity can interfere with this pressure-buffering function.

Elastic recoil helps sustain blood flow between heartbeats. Elastic arterial walls damp pulsatility and preserve downstream flow.

sections.guidingQuestion: Measure the pulse without confusing it with flow?
sections.explanation:
A pulse is the pressure wave produced when ventricular ejection distends arterial walls. At the wrist, the radial artery can be palpated gently with fingertips; the carotid pulse may be used with care, one side at a time and without strong pressure.

Count beats for a timed interval and convert to beats per minute, preferably after rest and with repeated trials. Compare manual counting with a validated optical sensor and note motion artefacts. Pulse rate estimates heart rate during a regular rhythm, but it is not the speed at which individual red cells travel.

If 18 beats occur in 15 seconds, the estimate is 72 beats min⁻¹. A pulse is an arterial pressure wave normally associated with each ventricular beat.

sections.explanation:
Blood in most systemic veins returns to the heart at comparatively low pressure. Vein walls are more compliant and readily compressed by surrounding skeletal muscles; valves in many peripheral veins help stop backward movement when the muscles relax.

Contraction of nearby muscles squeezes venous segments and propels blood toward the heart, with the direction constrained by valves. Respiratory pressure changes and the heart's pumping also contribute to venous return. Not all veins contain valves, so it is inaccurate to call valves universal.

Walking helps leg muscles assist venous return. Muscle compression and one-way valves assist venous return.

sections.explanation:
The coronary arteries supply the myocardium with oxygenated blood. Atherosclerotic plaques can narrow coronary vessels; plaque rupture with thrombus formation can abruptly obstruct flow. Insufficient oxygen supply causes myocardial ischaemia, and sustained severe obstruction can cause death of heart-muscle cells: myocardial infarction.

Epidemiological correlations between risk factors and coronary heart disease require careful interpretation. Smoking, blood pressure, plasma lipids, diabetes, socioeconomic conditions and age can be confounders. A high correlation coefficient describes association, not proof of a specific causal pathway; compare populations, methods and absolute rates.

A sudden thrombotic occlusion can interrupt oxygen delivery to myocardium. Coronary disease interpretation requires mechanistic evidence and carefully controlled population data.

sections.guidingQuestion: Cohesion and evaporation pull xylem water?
sections.explanation:
Water evaporates from moist mesophyll walls and leaves through stomata. The removal lowers local water potential and pulls replacement water from adjacent cell walls and xylem. The resulting tension (negative pressure potential) is transmitted downward through the xylem's cohesive column.

Hydrogen bonding supplies cohesion between water molecules, preventing the stretched column from fragmenting under ordinary conditions. Adhesion and capillary interactions help wet narrow walls and transfer water through cell-wall spaces, but evaporation-generated tension is the main driver of high-tree transport. No transpiration-powered pump is located at the roots.

A high, sunlit tree can move water upward without an ATP-powered xylem pump. Evaporation in leaves generates tension that pulls a continuous cohesive xylem column.

sections.guidingQuestion: Xylem vessel elements are built for tension?
sections.explanation:
Mature xylem vessel elements lose their protoplasts and become hollow conduits. Perforated or absent end walls connect vessel elements and minimize resistance to bulk water flow. They are not metabolically pumping water once mature.

Lignified secondary walls reinforce the conduit against collapse under negative pressure, often forming rings, helices or pits according to cell type. Pits in side walls allow lateral movement into adjacent conduits and surrounding cells. An embolism can block a vessel; redundant networks help maintain transport.

Lignin prevents a water-conducting conduit from imploding under tension. Hollow lignified vessels permit low-resistance water flow under negative pressure.

sections.guidingQuestion: Map vascular bundles in dicot stems?
sections.explanation:
A typical young dicot stem has an outer epidermis over cortex tissue and a ring of discrete vascular bundles. In each bundle, phloem is on the outer side toward the cortex and xylem on the inner side toward the pith; cambium may occur between them.

A low-power transverse plan should show the relative positions of epidermis, cortex, vascular bundles, pith and xylem versus phloem. Label tissue regions rather than inventing cell-level features not visible at that magnification. Use authentic stem micrographs to verify the pattern; atypical species may differ.

A young sunflower stem often shows vascular bundles arranged in a ring. Dicot stem bundles commonly form a peripheral ring with xylem inward and phloem outward.

sections.guidingQuestion: Recognize transport tissue in dicot roots?
sections.explanation:

Indicate xylem and phloem accurately and do not confuse the endodermis with the outer epidermis. Species and root age influence vascular anatomy; a teaching schematic expresses the typical case.

At the arteriole end of many capillary beds, hydrostatic pressure promotes passage of fluid and small dissolved solutes through the capillary wall into interstitial spaces. Blood cells and most large plasma proteins generally remain within intact capillaries; the interstitial fluid then bathes cells.

The syllabus describes lower venular pressure allowing some fluid re-entry. Modern revised Starling physiology emphasizes that sustained venular reabsorption is often limited in most systemic capillaries and lymphatics return much filtered volume. Present schematic pressure gradients as a simplified syllabus model while noting context, endothelial glycocalyx and tissue-specific exceptions.

Increased capillary hydrostatic pressure can promote oedema when drainage is inadequate. Fluid movement depends on hydrostatic and oncotic forces, with lymphatic return important.

sections.guidingQuestion: Tissue fluid exchanges with living cells?
sections.explanation:
Plasma is the liquid component of blood and contains dissolved nutrients, electrolytes and proteins. Tissue fluid is formed mainly by filtration of plasma; it has comparatively low concentrations of most large plasma proteins and normally lacks red blood cells. It occupies extracellular spaces around tissue cells.

Oxygen, glucose and other substrates move from capillary blood through interstitial fluid to cells, while carbon dioxide and metabolic wastes travel in reverse following gradients and transport processes. Not all exchanges are free passive diffusion, since specialized cell membrane carriers also matter. Cells depend on circulation to renew surrounding fluid.

A metabolically active cell obtains dissolved oxygen from nearby interstitial fluid. Interstitial fluid is protein-poorer than plasma and mediates material exchange.

sections.guidingQuestion: Lymphatic capillaries return excess tissue fluid?
sections.explanation:
Not all interstitial fluid returns directly to blood capillaries. Blind-ended lymphatic capillaries have thin endothelial walls with overlapping openings that allow excess fluid, proteins and some immune cells to enter. Once inside it is called lymph.

Lymphatic collecting vessels contain valves to restrict backflow, and surrounding muscle movement helps propel lymph through larger ducts that empty into the venous circulation. Failure of drainage can cause tissue swelling. Lymph is not pumped by a four-chambered organ in the same way that blood is.

Removal or blockage of lymphatics may cause persistent local oedema. Valved lymphatics collect interstitial fluid and return it to blood circulation.

sections.guidingQuestion: Single fish versus double mammalian circulation?
sections.explanation:
In bony fish, blood flows heart → gills → body tissues → heart in a single circuit. The heart pumps predominantly deoxygenated blood toward the gill capillaries, where oxygen is acquired before blood moves on to the tissues.

In mammals, blood flows through two circuits: right heart → lungs → left heart, then left heart → systemic tissues → right heart. Separation allows high pressure for systemic transport and lower pressure in the pulmonary bed. Draw flow with named organs and distinguish the direction of blood flow from its changing oxygen status.

Gill resistance lowers blood pressure before fish blood reaches systemic tissues. Fish have a single circulation; mammals have separate pulmonary and systemic circuits.

sections.guidingQuestion: Cardiac valves and chambers keep flow one-way?
sections.explanation:
The atria receive returning blood and send it to the ventricles; thick ventricular myocardium delivers blood under pressure into the pulmonary trunk and aorta. The septum prevents direct mixing of oxygenated and deoxygenated blood. Coronary vessels supply the working muscle itself.

Atrioventricular valves stop regurgitation from ventricles into atria, and semilunar valves prevent blood in large arteries returning into ventricles. The sinoatrial node initiates coordinated electrical activation. Trace venae cavae → right atrium → right ventricle → pulmonary artery → lungs → pulmonary veins → left atrium → left ventricle → aorta.

Closing AV valves during ventricular contraction helps preserve forward flow. Valves maintain directional flow, while myocardium generates pressure.

sections.guidingQuestion: Cardiac cycle: filling, pressure and ejection?
sections.explanation:
The sinoatrial node begins electrical excitation; atrial contraction completes ventricular filling. As ventricular myocardium contracts, ventricular pressure rises, closing atrioventricular valves. When ventricular pressure exceeds the aortic pressure, the aortic semilunar valve opens and blood is ejected.

During ventricular relaxation, falling pressure closes the aortic valve, and later the mitral valve opens as ventricular pressure drops below atrial pressure. Systolic blood pressure is the higher arterial pressure during ventricular ejection; diastolic pressure is the lower value during relaxation. A reading of 120/80 mmHg is an example, not a required norm.

A valve opens because pressure on its upstream side exceeds pressure downstream. Pressure changes determine valve state through the cardiac cycle.

sections.guidingQuestion: Root pressure operates when transpiration is weak?
sections.explanation:
Roots can accumulate mineral ions in xylem by active transport using energy from respiration. This decreases water potential in the xylem fluid and favours osmotic water movement from neighbouring root tissues.

Water entry can generate positive hydrostatic pressure in xylem, sometimes causing guttation or upward sap movement.
